claim: Schnyder corneal dystrophy (SCD) is an autosomal dominant disorder in humans characterized by abnormal accumulation of cholesterol in the cornea.
source: Schnyder corneal dystrophy (SCD) is an autosomal dominant disorder in humans characterized by abnormal accumulation of cholesterol in the cornea.
evidence: This is a well-established clinical characterization of SCD cited in the introduction and supported by references to prior literature.

claim: SCD-associated mutations have been identified in the gene encoding UBIAD1.
source: SCD-associated mutations have been identified in the gene encoding UBIAD1, a prenyltransferase that synthesizes vitamin K2.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior studies (Orr et al., 2007; Weiss et al., 2007) mentioned in the introduction.

claim: UBIAD1 is a prenyltransferase that synthesizes vitamin K2.
source: SCD-associated mutations have been identified in the gene encoding UBIAD1, a prenyltransferase that synthesizes vitamin K2.
evidence: This is supported by citations to biochemical studies (Nakagawa et al., 2010; Hirota et al., 2013) in the introduction.

claim: Sterols stimulate binding of UBIAD1 to HMG CoA reductase.
source: Here, we show that sterols stimulate binding of UBIAD1 to the cholesterol biosynthetic enzyme HMG CoA reductase, which is subject to sterol-accelerated, endoplasmic reticulum (ER)-associated degradation augmented by the nonsterol isoprenoid geranylgeraniol through an unknown mechanism.
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figures 3B, 3C, and related data.

claim: HMG CoA reductase is subject to sterol-accelerated, endoplasmic reticulum (ER)-associated degradation.
source: Here, we show that sterols stimulate binding of UBIAD1 to the cholesterol biosynthetic enzyme HMG CoA reductase, which is subject to sterol-accelerated, endoplasmic reticulum (ER)-associated degradation augmented by the nonsterol isoprenoid geranylgeraniol through an unknown mechanism.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by multiple citations in the introduction and background sections.

claim: Geranylgeraniol augments sterol-accelerated ER-associated degradation of HMG CoA reductase.
source: Here, we show that sterols stimulate binding of UBIAD1 to the cholesterol biosynthetic enzyme HMG CoA reductase, which is subject to sterol-accelerated, endoplasmic reticulum (ER)-associated degradation augmented by the nonsterol isoprenoid geranylgeraniol through an unknown mechanism.
evidence: This is supported by prior literature (Sever et al., 2003a) and confirmed by experimental data in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: Geranylgeraniol inhibits binding of UBIAD1 to reductase.
source: Geranylgeraniol inhibits binding of UBIAD1 to reductase, allowing its degradation and promoting transport of UBIAD1 from the ER to the Golgi.
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiments in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Geranylgeraniol promotes transport of UBIAD1 from the ER to the Golgi.
source: Geranylgeraniol inhibits binding of UBIAD1 to reductase, allowing its degradation and promoting transport of UBIAD1 from the ER to the Golgi.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplements 2 and 3.

claim: CRISPR-CAS9-mediated knockout of UBIAD1 relieves the geranylgeraniol requirement for reductase degradation.
source: CRISPR-CAS9-mediated knockout of UBIAD1 relieves the geranylgeraniol requirement for reductase degradation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments in Figure 6C and 6D showing complete degradation of reductase in UBIAD1− cells without geranylgeraniol.

claim: SCD-associated mutations in UBIAD1 block its displacement from reductase in the presence of geranylgeraniol.
source: SCD-associated mutations in UBIAD1 block its displacement from reductase in the presence of geranylgeraniol, thereby preventing degradation of reductase.
evidence: This is shown by co-immunoprecipitation experiments in Figure 8A and Figure 8—figure supplement 1 with UBIAD1 (N102S).

claim: SCD-associated mutations in UBIAD1 prevent degradation of reductase.
source: SCD-associated mutations in UBIAD1 block its displacement from reductase in the presence of geranylgeraniol, thereby preventing degradation of reductase.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments in Figure 7B and 7C showing stabilization of reductase by UBIAD1 (N102S) and (G177R).

claim: UBIAD1 is the target of geranylgeraniol in reductase degradation.
source: The current results identify UBIAD1 as the elusive target of geranylgeraniol in reductase degradation, the inhibition of which may contribute to accumulation of cholesterol in SCD.
evidence: This is the central finding of the study, supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence including knockout, knockdown, and binding studies.

claim: Inhibition of reductase degradation may contribute to accumulation of cholesterol in SCD.
source: The current results identify UBIAD1 as the elusive target of geranylgeraniol in reductase degradation, the inhibition of which may contribute to accumulation of cholesterol in SCD.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the experimental findings and the known cholesterol accumulation in SCD.

claim: The clinical manifestation of SCD can be apparent early in life, usually within the first decade.
source: The clinical manifestation of SCD can be apparent early in life, usually within the first decade.
evidence: This is a clinical observation cited from prior literature (Klintworth, 2009; Weiss, 2009).

claim: Approximately 50% of SCD patients ≥50 years of age undergo corneal transplant surgery for restoration of normal vision acuity.
source: The significance of this visual impairment is highlighted by the frequency in which corneal transplant surgery is utilized in treatment of SCD; approximately 50% of SCD patients ≥50 years of age undergo corneal transplant surgery for restoration of normal vision acuity (Weiss, 2007).
evidence: This is a clinical statistic cited from prior literature (Weiss, 2007).

claim: The frequency of corneal transplant surgery increases to greater than 70% for SCD patients 70 years and older.
source: The frequency of the procedure increases to greater than 70% for SCD patients 70 years and older.
evidence: This is a clinical statistic inferred from the context of the previous sentence citing Weiss, 2007.

claim: Corneas removed from SCD patients during transplantation surgery revealed a marked accumulation of unesterified cholesterol and lesser accumulation of esterified cholesterol and phospholipids.
source: Analyses of corneas removed from SCD patients during transplantation surgery revealed a marked accumulation of unesterified cholesterol and lesser accumulation of esterified cholesterol and phospholipids (McCarthy et al., 1994; Gaynor et al., 1996; Yamada et al., 1998), suggesting dysregulation of cholesterol metabolism may underlie pathogenesis of the disease.
evidence: This is supported by biochemical analyses cited from prior studies (McCarthy et al., 1994; Gaynor et al., 1996; Yamada et al., 1998).

claim: Dysregulation of cholesterol metabolism may underlie pathogenesis of SCD.
source: Analyses of corneas removed from SCD patients during transplantation surgery revealed a marked accumulation of unesterified cholesterol and lesser accumulation of esterified cholesterol and phospholipids (McCarthy et al., 1994; Gaynor et al., 1996; Yamada et al., 1998), suggesting dysregulation of cholesterol metabolism may underlie pathogenesis of the disease.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observed cholesterol accumulation in SCD corneas.

claim: Systemic dyslipidemia has been reported to be associated with some, but not all cases of SCD.
source: Systemic dyslipidemia has been reported to be associated with some, but not all cases of SCD (Thiel et al., 1977; Brownstein et al., 1991; Crispin, 2002).
evidence: This is a clinical observation cited from prior literature (Thiel et al., 1977; Brownstein et al., 1991; Crispin, 2002).

claim: In 2007, two groups independently identified SCD-associated mutations in the gene encoding UBIAD1.
source: In 2007, two groups independently identified SCD-associated mutations in the gene encoding UBIAD1 (UbiA prenyltransferase domain-containing protein-1) (Orr et al., 2007; Weiss et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a historical fact cited from the literature (Orr et al., 2007; Weiss et al., 2007).

claim: UBIAD1 was first described as being absent or markedly diminished in bladder and prostate tumors.
source: UBIAD1 (also known as TERE1) was first described as being absent or markedly diminished in bladder and prostate tumors (McGarvey et al., 2001, 2003) and belongs to the UbiA superfamily of prenyltransferases (Heide, 2009).
evidence: This is a historical observation cited from prior studies (McGarvey et al., 2001, 2003).

claim: UBIAD1 belongs to the UbiA superfamily of prenyltransferases.
source: UBIAD1 (also known as TERE1) was first described as being absent or markedly diminished in bladder and prostate tumors (McGarvey et al., 2001, 2003) and belongs to the UbiA superfamily of prenyltransferases (Heide, 2009).
evidence: This is a classification based on sequence and functional homology cited from the literature (Heide, 2009).

claim: UbiA prenyltransferases contain 8–10 transmembrane helices.
source: These enzymes, which are found in a wide variety of species, contain 8–10 transmembrane helices and catalyze transfer of isoprenyl groups to aromatic acceptors, producing a diverse range of molecules including ubiquinone, chlorophylls, hemes, vitamin E, and vitamin K (Forsgren et al., 2004; Nakagawa et al., 2010; Bonitz et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a structural characteristic of the enzyme family cited from the literature (Forsgren et al., 2004; Nakagawa et al., 2010; Bonitz et al., 2011).

claim: UbiA prenyltransferases catalyze transfer of isoprenyl groups to aromatic acceptors.
source: These enzymes, which are found in a wide variety of species, contain 8–10 transmembrane helices and catalyze transfer of isoprenyl groups to aromatic acceptors, producing a diverse range of molecules including ubiquinone, chlorophylls, hemes, vitamin E, and vitamin K (Forsgren et al., 2004; Nakagawa et al., 2010; Bonitz et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a biochemical function of the enzyme family cited from the literature (Forsgren et al., 2004; Nakagawa et al., 2010; Bonitz et al., 2011).

claim: UBIAD1 catalyzes transfer of the 20-carbon geranylgeranyl group from geranylgeranyl pyrophosphate to menadione (vitamin K3) derived from plant-derived phylloquinone (vitamin K1), generating MK-4 (menaquinone-4, vitamin K2).
source: Indeed, UBIAD1 catalyzes transfer of the 20-carbon geranylgeranyl group from geranylgeranyl pyrophosphate to menadione (vitamin K3) derived from plant-derived phylloquinone (vitamin K1), generating MK-4 (menaquinone-4, vitamin K2) (Figure 1) (Nakagawa et al., 2010; Hirota et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a biochemical reaction catalyzed by UBIAD1, supported by citations (Nakagawa et al., 2010; Hirota et al., 2013) and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: It has been proposed that UBIAD1 mediates polyprenylation of 4-hydroxybenzoate to produce 3-polyprenyl-4-hydroxybenzoate (PPHB), an intermediate in the synthesis of CoQ10 (coenzyme Q10 or ubiquinone-10).
source: It has also been proposed that UBIAD1 mediates polyprenylation of 4-hydroxybenzoate to produce 3-polyprenyl-4-hydroxybenzoate (PPHB), an intermediate in the synthesis of CoQ10 (coenzyme Q10 or ubiquinone-10) (Mugoni et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a proposed function of UBIAD1 cited from the literature (Mugoni et al., 2013).

claim: To date, 24 UBIAD1 mutations have been identified in ∼50 SCD families.
source: To date, 24 UBIAD1 mutations have been identified in ∼50 SCD families (Nickerson et al., 2013; Nowinska et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a summary of genetic findings cited from the literature (Nickerson et al., 2013; Nowinska et al., 2014).

claim: Several SCD-associated mutations alter amino acid residues that localize to the active site of the UBIAD1 prenyltransferase domain as determined by molecular modeling.
source: Several of these mutations alter amino acid residues that localize to the active site of the UBIAD1 prenyltransferase domain as determined by molecular modeling using structural models of bacterial and archaeal UbiA prenyltransferases (Bräuer et al., 2004, 2008; Nickerson et al., 2010; Cheng and Li, 2014; Huang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on computational modeling studies cited from the literature (Bräuer et al., 2004, 2008; Nickerson et al., 2010; Cheng and Li, 2014; Huang et al., 2014).

claim: Cells from patients harboring four SCD-associated mutations (N102S, D112N, and G177E/R) exhibited reduced MK-4 biosynthetic activity.
source: Cells from patients harboring four SCD-associated mutations (N102S, D112N, and G177E/R) exhibited reduced MK-4 biosynthetic activity (Nickerson et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a functional characterization of SCD mutations cited from the literature (Nickerson et al., 2013).

claim: Co-immunoprecipitation studies showed an association of UBIAD1 with HMG CoA reductase.
source: A possible link between UBIAD1 and cholesterol metabolism was provided by co-immunoprecipitation studies that showed an association of UBIAD1 with the cholesterol biosynthetic enzyme HMG CoA (3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl coenzyme A) reductase (Nickerson et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a biochemical observation cited from prior literature (Nickerson et al., 2013) and confirmed in the current study.

claim: The ER-localized reductase catalyzes reduction of HMG CoA to mevalonate.
source: In mammalian cells, the ER (endoplasmic reticulum)-localized reductase catalyzes reduction of HMG CoA to mevalonate (Figure 1).
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge about the function of HMG CoA reductase, illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: The reduction of HMG CoA to mevalonate constitutes a rate-limiting step in synthesis of cholesterol.
source: This reaction constitutes a rate-limiting step in synthesis of cholesterol as well as nonsterol isoprenoids such as the farnesyl and geranylgeranyl groups that are transferred to many cellular proteins and utilized in synthesis of ubiquinone, heme, and dolichol (Goldstein and Brown, 1990; Casey and Seabra, 1996).
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge cited from the literature (Goldstein and Brown, 1990; Casey and Seabra, 1996).

claim: Multiple feedback mechanisms converge on reductase to ensure a constant supply of nonsterol isoprenoids, while avoiding overaccumulation of cholesterol.
source: Multiple feedback mechanisms converge on reductase to ensure a constant supply of nonsterol isoprenoids, while avoiding overaccumulation of cholesterol (Brown and Goldstein, 1980).
evidence: This is a regulatory principle of cholesterol metabolism cited from the literature (Brown and Goldstein, 1980).

claim: Statins are competitive inhibitors of reductase that lower plasma levels of LDL-cholesterol and reduce the incidence of cardiovascular disease.
source: This feedback system is exploited therapeutically by a group of competitive inhibitors of reductase called statins, which trigger regulatory responses that result in the lowering of plasma levels of LDL (low-density lipoprotein)-cholesterol and thereby reduce the incidence of cardiovascular disease (Stossel, 2008; Marais et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge about statin therapy cited from the literature (Stossel, 2008; Marais et al., 2014).

claim: Statins block production of sterol and nonsterol isoprenoids that govern feedback regulation of reductase.
source: Statins also block production of sterol and nonsterol isoprenoids that govern feedback regulation of reductase (Goldstein and Brown, 1990).
evidence: This is a mechanistic consequence of statin action cited from the literature (Goldstein and Brown, 1990).

claim: A marked accumulation of reductase occurs in livers of statin-treated animals and humans.
source: Thus, a marked accumulation of reductase occurs in livers of statin-treated animals and humans (Brown and Goldstein, 1980; Kita et al., 1980; Reihner et al., 1990), which can blunt the cholesterol-lowering effects of these drugs.
evidence: This is an observed consequence of statin treatment cited from the literature (Brown and Goldstein, 1980; Kita et al., 1980; Reihner et al., 1990).

claim: Accumulation of reductase in statin-treated subjects can blunt the cholesterol-lowering effects of these drugs.
source: Thus, a marked accumulation of reductase occurs in livers of statin-treated animals and humans (Brown and Goldstein, 1980; Kita et al., 1980; Reihner et al., 1990), which can blunt the cholesterol-lowering effects of these drugs.
evidence: This is a clinical consequence inferred from the accumulation of reductase.

claim: Accumulation of reductase in statin-treated subjects results in part from slowed ERAD of reductase.
source: This accumulation results in part, from slowed ERAD (ER-associated degradation) of reductase (Nakanishi et al., 1988; Inoue et al., 1991; Ravid et al., 2000).
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation cited from the literature (Nakanishi et al., 1988; Inoue et al., 1991; Ravid et al., 2000).

claim: The ERAD of reductase is initiated by intracellular accumulation of sterols.
source: The ERAD of reductase is initiated by intracellular accumulation of sterols, which causes the enzyme to bind to ER membrane proteins called Insig-1 and Insig-2 (Sever et al., 2003a, 2003b) (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a mechanistic step in reductase ERAD cited from the literature (Sever et al., 2003a, 2003b) and illustrated in Figure 2.

claim: Sterols cause reductase to bind to ER membrane proteins called Insig-1 and Insig-2.
source: The ERAD of reductase is initiated by intracellular accumulation of sterols, which causes the enzyme to bind to ER membrane proteins called Insig-1 and Insig-2 (Sever et al., 2003a, 2003b) (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a mechanistic step in reductase ERAD cited from the literature (Sever et al., 2003a, 2003b) and illustrated in Figure 2.

claim: Insig binding occurs through the membrane domain of reductase, which contains eight membrane-spanning helices.
source: Insig binding occurs through the membrane domain of reductase, which contains eight membrane-spanning helices and precedes a large cytosolic domain with enzymatic activity (Liscum et al., 1985; Roitelman et al., 1992).
evidence: This is a structural and mechanistic detail cited from the literature (Liscum et al., 1985; Roitelman et al., 1992).

claim: Insig-associated ubiquitin ligases gp78 and Trc8 facilitate ubiquitination of cytosolically exposed lysine residues in the membrane domain of reductase.
source: Insig-associated ubiquitin ligases gp78 and Trc8 facilitate ubiquitination of cytosolically exposed lysine residues in the membrane domain of reductase (Sever et al., 2003a; Song et al., 2005; Jo et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a mechanistic step in reductase ERAD cited from the literature (Sever et al., 2003a; Song et al., 2005; Jo et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2012).

claim: Ubiquitination marks reductase for recognition by the AAA-ATPase VCP/p97, which mediates extraction of reductase across ER membranes.
source: This ubiquitination marks reductase for recognition by the AAA (ATPases associated with diverse cellular activities)-ATPase VCP/p97, which mediates extraction of reductase across ER membranes (Morris et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a mechanistic step in reductase ERAD cited from the literature (Morris et al., 2014).

claim: Once extracted, ubiquitinated reductase is released into the cytosol and delivered into the proteolytic chamber of the 20S proteasome.
source: Once extracted, ubiquitinated reductase is then released into the cytosol and delivered into the proteolytic chamber of the 20S proteasome through reactions mediated by the proteasome 19S regulatory particle, which contains six AAA-ATPases (Ehlinger and Walters, 2013).
evidence: This is a mechanistic step in protein degradation cited from the literature (Ehlinger and Walters, 2013).

claim: Geranylgeraniol augments sterol-accelerated ERAD of reductase but does not appreciably affect sterol-induced ubiquitination.
source: Geranylgeraniol, the alcohol derivative of geranylgeranyl pyrophosphate, augments sterol-accelerated ERAD of reductase but does not appreciably affect sterol-induced ubiquitination (Sever et al., 2003a).
evidence: This is an observation from prior literature (Sever et al., 2003a) that motivated the current study.

claim: Geranylgeraniol augments post-ubiquitination steps in reductase ERAD.
source: This observation led to the notion that geranylgeraniol augments post-ubiquitination steps in reductase ERAD (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on prior observations, illustrated in Figure 2.

claim: Geranylgeraniol enhances sterol-induced membrane extraction and cytosolic dislocation of reductase.
source: Indeed, geranylgeraniol enhances sterol-induced membrane extraction and cytosolic dislocation of reductase as judged by assays carried out in vitro and in intact cells (Song and DeBose-Boyd, 2004; Elsabrouty et al., 2013; Morris et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a mechanistic observation cited from the literature (Song and DeBose-Boyd, 2004; Elsabrouty et al., 2013; Morris et al., 2014).

claim: Proximity-dependent biotinylation was used to identify UBIAD1 as an associated protein of the membrane domain of reductase.
source: In the current studies, we use proximity-dependent biotinylation (Roux et al., 2012) to identify UBIAD1 as an associated protein of the membrane domain of reductase, which is necessary and sufficient for sterol-accelerated ERAD (Gil et al., 1985; Skalnik et al., 1988).
evidence: This is a methodological approach and finding of the current study, with the method cited from Roux et al., 2012.

claim: The membrane domain of reductase is necessary and sufficient for sterol-accelerated ERAD.
source: In the current studies, we use proximity-dependent biotinylation (Roux et al., 2012) to identify UBIAD1 as an associated protein of the membrane domain of reductase, which is necessary and sufficient for sterol-accelerated ERAD (Gil et al., 1985; Skalnik et al., 1988).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from the literature (Gil et al., 1985; Skalnik et al., 1988).

claim: Endogenous UBIAD1 binds to reductase in sterol-treated cells as determined by co-immunoprecipitation.
source: Endogenous UBIAD1 binds to reductase in sterol-treated cells as determined by co-immunoprecipitation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiments in Figure 3B and 3C.

claim: Geranylgeraniol-mediated displacement of UBIAD1 from reductase releases UBIAD1 for translocation from membranes of the ER to the Golgi.
source: This sterol-induced binding is inhibited by geranylgeraniol, releasing UBIAD1 for translocation from membranes of the ER to the Golgi.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence experiments in Figure 5C and related figures.

claim: RNAi-mediated knockdown of UBIAD1 relieves the geranylgeraniol requirement for reductase ERAD.
source: CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knockout and RNA interference (RNAi)-mediated knockdown of UBIAD1 relieves the geranylgeraniol requirement for reductase ERAD.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments in Figure 6A and 6B.

claim: UBIAD1 harboring the SCD-associated N102S mutation resists geranylgeraniol-mediated displacement from reductase.
source: UBIAD1 harboring the SCD-associated N102S mutation resists geranylgeraniol-mediated displacement from reductase and remains associated with the protein in the ER, thereby blocking sterol-accelerated degradation of reductase.
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiments in Figure 8A and Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: UBIAD1 (N102S) remains associated with reductase in the ER.
source: UBIAD1 harboring the SCD-associated N102S mutation resists geranylgeraniol-mediated displacement from reductase and remains associated with the protein in the ER, thereby blocking sterol-accelerated degradation of reductase.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence experiments in Figure 8B showing ER localization of UBIAD1 (N102S).

claim: UBIAD1 (N102S) blocks sterol-accelerated degradation of reductase.
source: UBIAD1 harboring the SCD-associated N102S mutation resists geranylgeraniol-mediated displacement from reductase and remains associated with the protein in the ER, thereby blocking sterol-accelerated degradation of reductase.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments in Figure 7B showing stabilization of reductase by UBIAD1 (N102S).

claim: Slowed ERAD of reductase may contribute to the accumulation of cholesterol observed in SCD.
source: These studies identify UBIAD1 as the elusive target of geranylgeraniol in the ERAD of reductase and provide insight into mechanisms through which the nonsterol isoprenoid modulates the reaction. Moreover, our results suggest that slowed ERAD of reductase may contribute to the accumulation of cholesterol observed in SCD.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the experimental findings linking UBIAD1 mutations to impaired reductase degradation.

claim: 25-HC triggered co-immunoprecipitation of endogenous reductase with Insig-1.
source: Immunoblot analysis revealed that treatment of cells with 25-HC triggered co-immunoprecipitation of endogenous reductase with Insig-1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, lanes 3 and 4); the control ER membrane protein calnexin failed to interact with reductase, regardless of the absence or presence of 25-HC (lanes 5 and 6).
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The control ER membrane protein calnexin failed to interact with reductase, regardless of the absence or presence of 25-HC.
source: Immunoblot analysis revealed that treatment of cells with 25-HC triggered co-immunoprecipitation of endogenous reductase with Insig-1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, lanes 3 and 4); the control ER membrane protein calnexin failed to interact with reductase, regardless of the absence or presence of 25-HC (lanes 5 and 6).
evidence: This is a negative control result shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B demonstrating specificity of the reductase-UBIAD1 interaction.

claim: ERGIC-53 failed to appear in the anti-reductase immunoprecipitates.
source: ERGIC-53 similarly failed to appear in the anti-reductase immunoprecipitates (lanes 9 and 10).
evidence: This is a negative control result shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Lamina-associated peptide-2 co-precipitated with reductase in both the absence and presence of 25-HC.
source: In contrast, lamina-associated peptide-2 (lanes 7 and 8), peroxiredoxin-4 (lanes 11 and 12), PGRMC2 (lanes 13 and 14), and annexin-A1 (lanes 15 and 16) co-precipitated with reductase in both the absence and presence of 25-HC; the significance and specificity of these interactions are unclear.
evidence: This is an observation from Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, though the authors note the significance is unclear.

claim: Peroxiredoxin-4 co-precipitated with reductase in both the absence and presence of 25-HC.
source: In contrast, lamina-associated peptide-2 (lanes 7 and 8), peroxiredoxin-4 (lanes 11 and 12), PGRMC2 (lanes 13 and 14), and annexin-A1 (lanes 15 and 16) co-precipitated with reductase in both the absence and presence of 25-HC; the significance and specificity of these interactions are unclear.
evidence: This is an observation from Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, though the authors note the significance is unclear.

claim: PGRMC2 co-precipitated with reductase in both the absence and presence of 25-HC.
source: In contrast, lamina-associated peptide-2 (lanes 7 and 8), peroxiredoxin-4 (lanes 11 and 12), PGRMC2 (lanes 13 and 14), and annexin-A1 (lanes 15 and 16) co-precipitated with reductase in both the absence and presence of 25-HC; the significance and specificity of these interactions are unclear.
evidence: This is an observation from Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, though the authors note the significance is unclear.

claim: Annexin-A1 co-precipitated with reductase in both the absence and presence of 25-HC.
source: In contrast, lamina-associated peptide-2 (lanes 7 and 8), peroxiredoxin-4 (lanes 11 and 12), PGRMC2 (lanes 13 and 14), and annexin-A1 (lanes 15 and 16) co-precipitated with reductase in both the absence and presence of 25-HC; the significance and specificity of these interactions are unclear.
evidence: This is an observation from Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, though the authors note the significance is unclear.

claim: In the absence of 25-HC, a small amount of UBIAD1 appeared in the pellet fraction of the reductase immunoprecipitation.
source: In the absence of 25-HC, a small amount of UBIAD1 (UbiA prenyltransferase domain-containing protein-1) appeared in the pellet fraction of the reductase immunoprecipitation (lane 17); this appearance was markedly enhanced when the cells were subjected to treatment with 25-HC (lane 18).
evidence: This is an observation from Figure 3—figure supplement 1B showing basal interaction between UBIAD1 and reductase.

claim: The appearance of UBIAD1 in the pellet fraction of the reductase immunoprecipitation was markedly enhanced when the cells were subjected to treatment with 25-HC.
source: In the absence of 25-HC, a small amount of UBIAD1 (UbiA prenyltransferase domain-containing protein-1) appeared in the pellet fraction of the reductase immunoprecipitation (lane 17); this appearance was markedly enhanced when the cells were subjected to treatment with 25-HC (lane 18).
evidence: This is an observation from Figure 3—figure supplement 1B showing sterol-induced enhancement of UBIAD1-reductase interaction.

claim: Human UBIAD1 is comprised of 338 amino acids.
source: Similar to other UbiA prenyltransferases, UBIAD1 is very hydrophobic; the human enzyme is comprised of 338 amino acids and is predicted to contain at least eight transmembrane helices (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a structural characteristic of UBIAD1 shown in Figure 3A.

claim: UBIAD1 is predicted to contain at least eight transmembrane helices.
source: Similar to other UbiA prenyltransferases, UBIAD1 is very hydrophobic; the human enzyme is comprised of 338 amino acids and is predicted to contain at least eight transmembrane helices (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a structural prediction shown in Figure 3A based on sequence analysis.

claim: 25-HC-mediated association of UBIAD1 with reductase was observed following treatment of cells for 30 min.
source: Immunoblot analysis of anti-reductase immunoprecipitates revealed co-precipitation of endogenous UBIAD1 with reductase following treatment of cells for 30 min with 25-HC (Figure 3B, top panel, lane 6).
evidence: This is a time-course observation from Figure 3B.

claim: Sterol-induced co-precipitation of UBIAD1 with reductase continued after prolonged incubation, even though the total amount of reductase was reduced by accelerated degradation.
source: This sterol-induced co-precipitation continued after prolonged incubation (top panel, lanes 7–14), even though the total amount of reductase was reduced by accelerated degradation (second and fourth panels, lanes 12 and 14).
evidence: This is an observation from Figure 3B showing persistent UBIAD1-reductase interaction despite reductase degradation.

claim: The structurally related 1,1-bisphosphonate esters SR-12813 and Apomine mimic 25-HC in accelerating reductase ubiquitination and degradation.
source: The structurally related 1,1-bisphosphonate esters SR-12813 and Apomine mimic 25-HC in accelerating reductase ubiquitination and degradation (Roitelman et al., 2004; Sever et al., 2004; Nguyen et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from the literature (Roitelman et al., 2004; Sever et al., 2004; Nguyen et al., 2009).

claim: Apomine triggered co-precipitation between reductase and UBIAD1 in a manner similar to that of 25-HC.
source: As shown in Figure 3C, Apomine triggered co-precipitation between reductase and UBIAD1 in a manner similar to that of 25-HC (second panel, compare lane 2 with lanes 3–5).
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiments in Figure 3C.

claim: 25-HC stimulated co-precipitation of both UBIAD1 and Insig-1 with reductase in SV-589 cells transfected with control GFP siRNA.
source: Immunoblotting of precipitated proteins revealed that 25-HC stimulated co-precipitation of both UBIAD1 and Insig-1 with reductase in SV-589 cells transfected with control GFP siRNA (Figure 4A, second and third panels, lane 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiments in Figure 4A.

claim: The sterol-induced co-precipitation of UBIAD1 with reductase was markedly reduced in cells that received siRNAs against Insig-1 and Insig-2.
source: The sterol-induced co-precipitation of UBIAD1 with reductase was markedly reduced in cells that received siRNAs against Insig-1 and Insig-2 (second panel, lanes 3 and 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNAi experiments in Figure 4A showing Insig-dependence of UBIAD1-reductase interaction.

claim: Knockdown of UBIAD1 reduced, but did not eliminate the sterol-induced binding of reductase to Insig-1.
source: The experiment of Figure 4B shows that knockdown of UBIAD1 reduced, but did not eliminate the sterol-induced binding of reductase to Insig-1 (third panel, compare lanes 2 and 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNAi experiments in Figure 4B.

claim: RNAi-mediated knockdown of reductase abolished co-precipitation of Insig-1 with UBIAD1.
source: However, RNAi-mediated knockdown of reductase abolished co-precipitation of Insig-1 with UBIAD1 (bottom panel, compare lane 4 with lane 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNAi experiments in Figure 4C showing reductase-dependence of UBIAD1-Insig-1 interaction.

claim: Reductase and Insig-1 co-precipitated with UBIAD1 when control siRNA-transfected cells were treated with 25-HC.
source: Immunoblot analysis of anti-UBIAD1 immunoprecipitates revealed that as expected, reductase and Insig-1 co-precipitated with UBIAD1 when control siRNA-transfected cells were treated with 25-HC (Figure 4C, top and bottom panels, lane 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiments in Figure 4C.

claim: The proteasome inhibitor MG-132 blocked 25-HC-stimulated reductase degradation.
source: Immunoblot analysis of anti-reductase immunoprecipitates from lysates of cells treated in the absence of MG-132 shows that 25-HC stimulated reductase degradation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, top panel, compare lanes 1 and 2), which was blocked by MG-132 (lanes 3 and 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A using the proteasome inhibitor MG-132.

claim: Insig-1 co-precipitated with reductase in the presence of 25-HC, and this co-precipitation was enhanced by MG-132.
source: Insig-1 co-precipitated with reductase in the presence of 25-HC (second panel, lane 2) and this co-precipitation was enhanced by MG-132 (lane 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: UBIAD1 co-precipitated with reductase in 25-HC-treated cells; however, the interaction was reduced, rather than enhanced, in the presence of MG-132.
source: UBIAD1 also co-precipitated with reductase in 25-HC-treated cells (third panel, lane 2); however, the interaction was reduced, rather than enhanced, in the presence of MG-132 (lane 4).
evidence: This is an observation from Figure 5—figure supplement 1A suggesting UBIAD1 dissociates from reductase during or after ubiquitination.

claim: 25-HC dose-dependently stimulated co-precipitation of UBIAD1 with reductase.
source: As expected, 25-HC dose-dependently stimulated co-precipitation of UBIAD1 with reductase (Figure 5A, top panel, lanes a–c); however, this sterol-regulated association was inhibited in the presence of 10 or 20 µM geranylgeraniol (lanes d–i).
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiments in Figure 5A.

claim: Sterol-regulated association of UBIAD1 with reductase was inhibited in the presence of 10 or 20 µM geranylgeraniol.
source: As expected, 25-HC dose-dependently stimulated co-precipitation of UBIAD1 with reductase (Figure 5A, top panel, lanes a–c); however, this sterol-regulated association was inhibited in the presence of 10 or 20 µM geranylgeraniol (lanes d–i).
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiments in Figure 5A showing geranylgeraniol inhibits UBIAD1-reductase binding.

claim: Sterol-induced binding of UBIAD1 to reductase continued in the presence of 20 µM farnesol.
source: In contrast, sterol-induced binding of UBIAD1 to reductase continued in the presence of 20 µM farnesol (Figure 5B, top panel, compare lanes a–d with lanes e–h), a 15-carbon nonsterol isoprenoid that does not augment sterol-accelerated ERAD of reductase (Sever et al., 2003a).
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiments in Figure 5B showing specificity for geranylgeraniol.

claim: Farnesol is a 15-carbon nonsterol isoprenoid that does not augment sterol-accelerated ERAD of reductase.
source: In contrast, sterol-induced binding of UBIAD1 to reductase continued in the presence of 20 µM farnesol (Figure 5B, top panel, compare lanes a–d with lanes e–h), a 15-carbon nonsterol isoprenoid that does not augment sterol-accelerated ERAD of reductase (Sever et al., 2003a).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from the literature (Sever et al., 2003a).

claim: Endogenous UBIAD1 localized to juxtanuclear structures that resembled the Golgi and also stained with antibodies against the Golgi protein GM130 in SV-589 cells grown in medium containing FCS.
source: The results show that endogenous UBIAD1 localized to juxtanuclear structures that resembled the Golgi and also stained with antibodies against the Golgi protein GM130 (Nakamura et al., 1995) (Figure 5C, panels 1 and 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence experiments in Figure 5C.

claim: The Golgi localization of UBIAD1 was markedly diminished when the cells were depleted of sterol and nonsterol isoprenoids through incubation in medium containing LPPS and the reductase inhibitor compactin.
source: The Golgi localization of UBIAD1 was markedly diminished when the cells were depleted of sterol and nonsterol isoprenoids through incubation in medium containing LPPS (lipoprotein-poor serum) and the reductase inhibitor compactin (Figure 5C, panels 3 and 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence experiments in Figure 5C.

claim: Localization of Golgi-localized GM130 was unaffected by depletion of sterol and nonsterol isoprenoids.
source: Notably, localization of Golgi-localized GM130 was unaffected by depletion of sterol and nonsterol isoprenoids (compare panels 2 and 4).
evidence: This is a control observation from Figure 5C showing specificity of UBIAD1 relocalization.

claim: The Golgi localization of UBIAD1 was restored in sterol- and nonsterol isoprenoid-depleted cells by the addition of geranylgeraniol.
source: The Golgi localization of UBIAD1 was restored in sterol- and nonsterol isoprenoid-depleted cells by the addition of geranylgeraniol (Figure 5C, panel 5), but not by the addition of 25-HC (panel 7).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence experiments in Figure 5C.

claim: The Golgi localization of UBIAD1 was not restored in sterol- and nonsterol isoprenoid-depleted cells by the addition of 25-HC.
source: The Golgi localization of UBIAD1 was restored in sterol- and nonsterol isoprenoid-depleted cells by the addition of geranylgeraniol (Figure 5C, panel 5), but not by the addition of 25-HC (panel 7).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence experiments in Figure 5C.

claim: Sterol and nonsterol isoprenoid depletion disrupted the Golgi localization of UBIAD1, and this localization was restored by geranylgeraniol, but not by farnesol, 25-HC, or cholesterol.
source: A repeat experiment confirms that sterol and nonsterol isoprenoid depletion disrupted the Golgi localization of UBIAD1 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2). Importantly, this localization was restored by geranylgeraniol, but not by farnesol, 25-HC, or cholesterol.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence experiments in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Depletion of sterol and nonsterol isoprenoids disrupted Golgi localization of transfected Myc-UBIAD1, and this localization was restored by geranylgeraniol, but not by farnesol or 25-HC.
source: Depletion of sterol and nonsterol isoprenoids disrupted Golgi localization of transfected Myc-UBIAD1 (Figure 5—figure supplement 3). This localization was restored by geranylgeraniol, but not by farnesol or 25-HC.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence experiments in Figure 5—figure supplement 3 with transfected Myc-UBIAD1.

claim: Endogenous UBIAD1 exhibited relatively more non-Golgi staining compared to Myc-UBIAD1 in FCS-cultured cells, suggesting anti-Myc may have a greater degree of specificity compared to that of anti-UBIAD1.
source: Notably, endogenous UBIAD1 exhibited relatively more non-Golgi staining compared to Myc-UBIAD1 in FCS-cultured cells, suggesting anti-Myc may have a greater degree of specificity compared to that of anti-UBIAD1.
evidence: This is an observation comparing endogenous and transfected UBIAD1 localization, suggesting a technical consideration about antibody specificity.

claim: In wild type SV-589 cells, 25-HC stimulated reductase degradation from membranes, and this degradation was enhanced by geranylgeraniol.
source: Figure 6A shows that 25-HC stimulated reductase degradation from membranes of control siRNA-transfected cells (top panel, lane 2); this degradation was enhanced by geranylgeraniol (lanes 3 and 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated by subcellular fractionation experiments in Figure 6A.

claim: In UBIAD1 knockdown cells, 25-HC stimulated complete degradation of reductase, even in the absence of geranylgeraniol.
source: In UBIAD1 knockdown cells, 25-HC stimulated complete degradation of reductase, even in the absence of geranylgeraniol (lanes 5–8).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNAi experiments in Figure 6A showing UBIAD1 is required for the geranylgeraniol effect.

claim: Geranylgeraniol augmented the ERAD of reductase that was stimulated by Apomine.
source: Geranylgeraniol also augmented the ERAD of reductase that was stimulated by Apomine (Figure 6B, top panel, lanes 1–4); however, the 1,1-bisphosphonate ester caused reductase to become completely degraded in UBIAD1 knockdown cells (lanes 5–8).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments in Figure 6B.

claim: Apomine caused reductase to become completely degraded in UBIAD1 knockdown cells.
source: Geranylgeraniol also augmented the ERAD of reductase that was stimulated by Apomine (Figure 6B, top panel, lanes 1–4); however, the 1,1-bisphosphonate ester caused reductase to become completely degraded in UBIAD1 knockdown cells (lanes 5–8).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNAi experiments in Figure 6B.

claim: In wild type SV-589 cells, Apomine stimulated reductase ERAD through a mechanism augmented by geranylgeraniol.
source: In wild type SV-589 cells, Apomine stimulated reductase ERAD through a mechanism augmented by geranylgeraniol (Figure 6C, top panel, lanes 1–4), whereas the compound caused complete degradation of reductase in cells deficient in UBIAD1 (designated UBIAD1−) (lanes 5–8).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments in Figure 6C using CRISPR/Cas9 knockout cells.

claim: Apomine caused complete degradation of reductase in cells deficient in UBIAD1 (designated UBIAD1−).
source: In wild type SV-589 cells, Apomine stimulated reductase ERAD through a mechanism augmented by geranylgeraniol (Figure 6C, top panel, lanes 1–4), whereas the compound caused complete degradation of reductase in cells deficient in UBIAD1 (designated UBIAD1−) (lanes 5–8).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments in Figure 6C using CRISPR/Cas9 knockout cells.

claim: In a time-dependent fashion, geranylgeraniol augmented Apomine-induced degradation of reductase in SV-589 cells.
source: Figure 6D shows that in a time-dependent fashion, geranylgeraniol augmented Apomine-induced degradation of reductase in SV-589 cells (compare lanes 1–6 with lanes 7–12).
evidence: This is demonstrated by time-course experiments in Figure 6D.

claim: Apomine alone caused complete degradation of reductase in UBIAD1− cells, and augmentation by geranylgeraniol was markedly diminished.
source: However, Apomine alone caused complete degradation of reductase in UBIAD1− cells (Figure 6D, lanes 13–18) and augmentation by geranylgeraniol was markedly diminished (lanes 19–24).
evidence: This is demonstrated by time-course experiments in Figure 6D using UBIAD1− cells.

claim: Transfection of UBIAD1− cells with pCMV-Myc-UBIAD1 restored the requirement of geranylgeraniol for maximal degradation of reductase.
source: Importantly, transfection of UBIAD1− cells with pCMV-Myc-UBIAD1 restored the requirement of geranylgeraniol for maximal degradation of reductase (Figure 6E, top panel, compare lanes 1–3 with lanes 4–6).
evidence: This is a rescue experiment shown in Figure 6E demonstrating that UBIAD1 is responsible for the geranylgeraniol effect.

claim: Asparagine-102 (N102) is the most frequently altered UBIAD1 residue in SCD families.
source: Asparagine-102 (N102), which localizes to the prenyltransferase domain of UBIAD1 (Cheng and Li, 2014; Huang et al., 2014), is the most frequently altered residue (∼30%) in SCD families.
evidence: This is a summary of genetic findings from SCD families cited from the literature (Cheng and Li, 2014; Huang et al., 2014).

claim: N102 localizes to the prenyltransferase domain of UBIAD1.
source: Asparagine-102 (N102), which localizes to the prenyltransferase domain of UBIAD1 (Cheng and Li, 2014; Huang et al., 2014), is the most frequently altered residue (∼30%) in SCD families.
evidence: This is based on structural studies cited from the literature (Cheng and Li, 2014; Huang et al., 2014).

claim: SCD is an autosomal dominant disorder.
source: Considering that SCD is an autosomal dominant disorder, we reasoned that overexpression of UBIAD1 harboring the SCD-associated N102S mutation would block reductase ERAD.
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge about the inheritance pattern of SCD.

claim: When overexpressed in SV-589 cells, the T7-tagged membrane domain of reductase became degraded in the presence of 25-HC and geranylgeraniol.
source: Figure 7A shows that when overexpressed in SV-589 cells, the T7-tagged membrane domain of reductase became degraded in the presence of 25-HC and geranylgeraniol (top panel, lanes 1 and 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by transfection experiments in Figure 7A.

claim: Co-expression of a plasmid encoding wild type UBIAD1 stabilized reductase in a dose-dependent fashion and 25-HC plus geranylgeraniol continued to accelerate its ERAD.
source: Co-expression of a plasmid encoding wild type UBIAD1 stabilized reductase in a dose-dependent fashion and 25-HC plus geranylgeraniol continued to accelerate its ERAD (lanes 3–10).
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-transfection experiments in Figure 7A.

claim: The highest level of wild type UBIAD1 co-expressed with reductase blunted the enzyme's accelerated degradation.
source: Notably, the highest level of wild type UBIAD1 co-expressed with reductase blunted the enzyme's accelerated degradation (lanes 11 and 12).
evidence: This is an observation from Figure 7A showing that overexpression of wild type UBIAD1 can inhibit reductase degradation.

claim: Co-expression of UBIAD1 (N102S) stabilized the membrane domain of reductase.
source: Co-expression of UBIAD1 (N102S) also stabilized the membrane domain of reductase (Figure 7B, top panel, compare lane 1 with lanes 3, 5, 7, 9, and 11), suggesting the protein continued to bind to the enzyme.
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-transfection experiments in Figure 7B.

claim: UBIAD1 (N102S) blunted sterol-accelerated ERAD of reductase, even at low levels of expression.
source: However, UBIAD1 (N102S) blunted sterol-accelerated ERAD of reductase, even at low levels of expression (Figure 7B, top panel, compare lane 2 with lanes 4, 8, 10, and 12).
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-transfection experiments in Figure 7B showing dominant-negative effect of UBIAD1 (N102S).

claim: T7-tagged, full-length reductase was subjected to sterol-accelerated degradation when transfected alone or together with up to 100 ng of plasmid encoding wild type UBIAD1.
source: The protein was subjected to sterol-accelerated degradation when transfected alone or together with up to 100 ng of plasmid encoding wild type UBIAD1 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A, top panel, lanes 1–8); co-transfection of higher levels (300 and 1000 ng) of the UBIAD1-encoding plasmid inhibited reductase degradation (lanes 9–12).
evidence: This is demonstrated by transfection experiments in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A with full-length reductase.

claim: Co-transfection of higher levels (300 and 1000 ng) of the UBIAD1-encoding plasmid inhibited reductase degradation.
source: The protein was subjected to sterol-accelerated degradation when transfected alone or together with up to 100 ng of plasmid encoding wild type UBIAD1 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A, top panel, lanes 1–8); co-transfection of higher levels (300 and 1000 ng) of the UBIAD1-encoding plasmid inhibited reductase degradation (lanes 9–12).
evidence: This is demonstrated by transfection experiments in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Inhibition of full-length reductase degradation was observed upon co-transfection with a significantly lower amount (30 ng) of plasmid encoding UBIAD1 (N102S).
source: Consistent with results obtained with the reductase membrane domain, inhibition of full-length reductase degradation was observed upon co-transfection with a significantly lower amount (30 ng) of plasmid encoding UBIAD1 (N102S) (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B, top panel, compare lanes 1–4 with lanes 5–12).
evidence: This is demonstrated by transfection experiments in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B showing enhanced inhibitory effect of UBIAD1 (N102S).

claim: Glycine-177 (G177) is the second-most frequently altered UBIAD1 residue in SCD families.
source: Glycine-177 (G177, see Figure 3A) is the second-most frequently altered UBIAD1 residue in SCD families (Nickerson et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a summary of genetic findings from SCD families cited from the literature (Nickerson et al., 2013).

claim: UBAID1 harboring the SCD-associated G177R mutation blocked reductase ERAD to a degree similar to that observed with UBIAD1 (N102S).
source: The results of Figure 7C show that UBAID1 harboring the SCD-associated G177R mutation blocked reductase ERAD to a degree similar to that observed with UBIAD1 (N102S) (top panel, compare lanes 1 and 2 with lanes 3–6).
evidence: This is demonstrated by transfection experiments in Figure 7C.

claim: Wild type UBIAD1 co-precipitated with reductase in the 25-HC-treated cells, and this co-precipitation was inhibited by geranylgeraniol.
source: The results show that wild type UBIAD1 co-precipitated with reductase in the 25-HC-treated cells (Figure 8A, second panel, lane e). This co-precipitation was inhibited by geranylgeraniol (lanes g and h).
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiments in Figure 8A.

claim: UBIAD1 (N102S) co-precipitated with reductase; however, the mutant UBAID1 resisted geranylgeraniol-mediated displacement and remained associated with reductase.
source: UBIAD1 (N102S) similarly co-precipitated with reductase (lane i); however, the mutant UBAID1 resisted geranylgeraniol-mediated displacement and remained associated with reductase (lanes j–l).
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiments in Figure 8A showing the key defect in UBIAD1 (N102S).

claim: Wild type UBIAD1 localized to Golgi membranes that also stained with antibodies against GM130 in SV-589 cells grown in FCS-containing medium.
source: The results show that wild type UBIAD1 localized to Golgi membranes that also stained with antibodies against GM130 (Figure 8B, panels 1–4).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence experiments in Figure 8B.

claim: UBIAD1 (N102S) primarily exhibited a diffuse, reticular localization corresponding to ER membranes and little, if any, of the protein appeared in the Golgi.
source: UBIAD1 (N102S) primarily exhibited a diffuse, reticular localization corresponding to ER membranes and little, if any, of the protein appeared in the Golgi (Figure 8B, panels 5–8).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence experiments in Figure 8B showing mislocalization of UBIAD1 (N102S).

claim: UBIAD1 (G177R) was primarily concentrated in membranes of the ER, but not the Golgi.
source: Similar to the N102 mutant, UBIAD1 (G177R) was also primarily concentrated in membranes of the ER, but not the Golgi (Figure 8B, panels 9–12).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence experiments in Figure 8B showing mislocalization of UBIAD1 (G177R).

claim: Geranylgeraniol becomes phosphorylated to produce geranylgeranyl pyrophosphate.
source: In sterol-deprived cells, both reductase and UBIAD1 localize to membranes of the ER. The intracellular accumulation of sterols in ER membranes triggers binding of reductase to Insigs, resulting in its ubiquitination by Insig-associated ubiquitin ligases gp78 and Trc8 and association with UBIAD1. Geranylgeraniol becomes phosphorylated to produce geranylgeranyl pyrophosphate, which enhances reductase degradation by binding to UBIAD1, causing its displacement from reductase-Insig.
evidence: This is a mechanistic inference based on the known metabolism of geranylgeraniol and the model proposed in Figure 9.

claim: Geranylgeranyl pyrophosphate enhances reductase degradation by binding to UBIAD1, causing its displacement from reductase-Insig.
source: Geranylgeraniol becomes phosphorylated to produce geranylgeranyl pyrophosphate, which enhances reductase degradation by binding to UBIAD1, causing its displacement from reductase-Insig.
evidence: This is the proposed mechanism shown in Figure 9 based on the experimental findings.

claim: The SCD-associated N102S or G177R mutations in UBIAD1 abrogate binding of geranylgeranyl pyrophosphate.
source: We postulate that the SCD-associated N102S or G177R mutations in UBIAD1 abrogate binding of geranylgeranyl pyrophosphate.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed to explain the experimental observations with UBIAD1 mutants.

claim: UBIAD1 (N102S) and (G177R) do not translocate to the Golgi and remain associated with reductase in the ER.
source: As a result, UBIAD1 (N102S) and (G177R) do not translocate to the Golgi and remain associated with reductase in the ER, thereby blocking its membrane extraction, cytosolic dislocation, and proteasomal degradation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence and co-immunoprecipitation experiments in Figure 8.

claim: UBIAD1 (N102S) and (G177R) block membrane extraction, cytosolic dislocation, and proteasomal degradation of reductase.
source: As a result, UBIAD1 (N102S) and (G177R) do not translocate to the Golgi and remain associated with reductase in the ER, thereby blocking its membrane extraction, cytosolic dislocation, and proteasomal degradation.
evidence: This is a mechanistic conclusion based on the experimental findings in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: In the absence of LDL, cells accumulate reductase to produce mevalonate for conversion into primarily cholesterol and other sterols.
source: In 1979, Faust, Brown, and Goldstein found that in the absence of LDL, cells accumulate reductase to produce mevalonate for conversion into primarily cholesterol and other sterols (Faust et al., 1979).
evidence: This is a historical observation cited from the literature (Faust et al., 1979).

claim: The addition of LDL to cells partially suppressed reductase, limiting production of mevalonate.
source: The addition of LDL to cells partially suppressed reductase, limiting production of mevalonate.
evidence: This is a regulatory observation from the literature (Faust et al., 1979).

claim: When LDL is added to cells, incorporation of mevalonate into cholesterol was reduced, whereas incorporation of the molecule into nonsterol isoprenoids such as CoQ10 was enhanced.
source: As a result, incorporation of mevalonate into cholesterol was reduced, whereas incorporation of the molecule into nonsterol isoprenoids such as CoQ10 was enhanced.
evidence: This is a metabolic observation from the literature (Faust et al., 1979).

claim: LDL failed to completely suppress reductase due to its binding to UBIAD1 and resultant inhibition of sterol-accelerated degradation.
source: We postulate that LDL failed to completely suppress reductase due to its binding to UBIAD1 and resultant inhibition of sterol-accelerated degradation.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed to explain the incomplete suppression of reductase by LDL.

claim: Residual reductase produces a small amount of mevalonate that is preferentially diverted into nonsterol isoprenoids.
source: This residual reductase produces a small amount of mevalonate that is preferentially diverted into nonsterol isoprenoids.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about metabolic channeling based on the proposed model.

claim: Once appropriate levels of geranylgeranyl pyrophosphate accumulate in cells, the isoprenoid binds to UBIAD1, causing its release from reductase, which subsequently becomes degraded.
source: Once appropriate levels of geranylgeranyl pyrophosphate accumulate in cells, the isoprenoid binds to UBIAD1, causing its release from reductase, which subsequently becomes degraded.
evidence: This is a proposed regulatory mechanism based on the experimental findings.

claim: Released UBIAD1 translocates to the Golgi where it synthesizes PPHB and perhaps MK-4.
source: Released UBIAD1 then translocates to the Golgi where it synthesizes PPHB (Mugoni et al., 2013) and perhaps MK-4.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about UBIAD1 function in the Golgi, with PPHB synthesis cited from Mugoni et al., 2013.

claim: Substrate-regulated transport of UBIAD1 ensures that products of the enzyme are only produced when cellular demands for other nonsterol isoprenoids as well as sterols have been met.
source: Thus, substrate-regulated transport of UBIAD1 ensures that products of the enzyme are only produced when cellular demands for other nonsterol isoprenoids as well as sterols have been met.
evidence: This is a proposed regulatory principle based on the experimental findings and model.

claim: Mutation of the asparagine residue in bacterial UbiA prenyltransferases that corresponds to N102 markedly diminishes substrate binding and enzymatic activity.
source: Mutation of the asparagine residue in bacterial UbiA prenyltransferases that corresponds to N102 markedly diminishes substrate binding and enzymatic activity (Cheng and Li, 2014; Huang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a functional observation from bacterial enzymes cited from the literature (Cheng and Li, 2014; Huang et al., 2014).

claim: Binding of UBIAD1 to geranylgeranyl pyrophosphate produced by phosphorylation of geranylgeraniol triggers displacement of wild type UBIAD1 from reductase, allowing the protein to translocate to the Golgi.
source: Thus, we postulate that binding of UBIAD1 to geranylgeranyl pyrophosphate produced by phosphorylation of geranylgeraniol triggers displacement of wild type UBIAD1 from reductase, allowing the protein to translocate to the Golgi.
evidence: This is a mechanistic hypothesis based on the experimental findings.

claim: The N102S and G177R mutants of UBIAD1 exhibit reduced affinity for geranylgeranyl pyrophosphate.
source: In contrast, the N102S and G177R mutants of UBIAD1 exhibit reduced affinity for geranylgeranyl pyrophosphate and thus, remain associated with reductase in the ER, thereby inhibiting its sterol-accelerated ERAD (Figure 9).
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed to explain the behavior of UBIAD1 mutants, illustrated in Figure 9.

claim: The N102S and G177R mutants of UBIAD1 remain associated with reductase in the ER, thereby inhibiting its sterol-accelerated ERAD.
source: In contrast, the N102S and G177R mutants of UBIAD1 exhibit reduced affinity for geranylgeranyl pyrophosphate and thus, remain associated with reductase in the ER, thereby inhibiting its sterol-accelerated ERAD (Figure 9).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments in Figures 7 and 8 and summarized in the model in Figure 9.

claim: Inhibition of reductase ERAD by UBIAD1 mutants may contribute to the accumulation of cholesterol that is observed in corneas of SCD patients.
source: This inhibition may contribute to the accumulation of cholesterol that is observed in corneas of SCD patients.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion linking the molecular findings to the clinical phenotype of SCD.
